extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; readers of philosophy/epistemology of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to define, justify, and use causal claims and probabilistic proof in empirical science — distinguishing routine/perception from conceptual necessity and giving rules for when to accept/reject causal inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid postulating first causes (reject metaphysical 'will')
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the conception of 'will' or a first cause is invoked as an arbitrary originator or enforcer of a sequence, science should replace that assertion with the admission 'Here, for the present, our ignorance begins.' Science knows nothing of first causes; they cannot be inferred from scientific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer unobservable 'first causes' from scientific data; treat such invocations as marks of ignorance or as metaphysical hypotheses. Prefer to state limits of current knowledge rather than posit inexplicable originating agents (example: rejecting Paley-style separate creation claims or souls as first causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define cause as a stage in a routine of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a sequence of perceptions D, E, F, G is invariably preceded by the perception C (i.e. the perceptions always occur in that order, forming a routine of experience), C is said to be a cause of D, E, F, G; those are its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'cause' as an empirical marker of invariant antecedence in repeated observation (a stage in a routine), not as something that 'originates' or 'enforces' by inherent necessity. Use examples (random number series vs arithmetic progressions) to distinguish mere repetition/routine from logical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiplicity and succession of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: No phenomenon or stage in a sequence has only one cause; all antecedent stages are successive causes and the succession can be carried back to the limit of existing knowledge (and beyond in conceivable knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing causes, enumerate successive antecedent stages as contributing causes rather than seeking a single ultimate cause. Accept that tracing causes can lead back indefinitely and science will usually trace one manageable line or range of causes for general descriptive purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of the elastic 'width' of cause and limit practical tracing
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'cause' can be widened (e.g., causes of an ash-tree's growth might include garden, metropolis, geological history). To know all causes would be to know the universe; science must content itself with tracing one line/range of causes for general types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting impossible total causal histories for individual, particular objects; focus on general causes for classes (e.g., ash-trees generally) that are useful for scientific description and prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concise descriptions of motions to invoking vague 'forces'
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphysical conception 'force' (mechanical/vital/social forces) often symbolizes mental obscurity; sequences we deal with are reducible to descriptions of motion or change, and 'force' frequently hides knowledge rather than provides it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce phenomena to analyzable sequences of change/motion (chemical, physical, physiological descriptions) rather than appealing to ill-defined 'forces.' Use precise mechanisms and measurable descriptions where available to avoid obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish necessity in conception from necessity in perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty and logical necessity belong to the world of conceptions (definitions, axioms); they do not exist in the sequence of sense-impressions. A theory may be logically necessary internally, but that does not make perceptual sequences inherently necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate mathematical or conceptual necessity (e.g., circle theorems) with empirical inevitability. Treat theories as conceptual frameworks whose logical consequences can be tested against perceptions; if perceptions disagree, the theory fails as a descriptive model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require routine in perception as a condition of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition or routine in perceptions (the same set of causes being always accompanied by the same effect) is an essential condition of thought and for prediction; without invariable order knowledge and thought become impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, check whether regularity/routine is present in the perceptual data; absence of stable routines undermines the basis for making predictions or forming scientific knowledge. Emphasize reproducibility and consistent sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat empirical 'proof' as probabilistic rather than absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'provable' in the perceptual/empirical sphere corresponds to 'probable'; proof as demonstrable certainty applies only to conceptions. When 'prove' is used about phenomena it implicitly means extreme probability based on routine of perceptions, not absolute demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame empirical claims and 'proofs' in probabilistic terms. Require sufficient repeated and class-level experience before treating an empirical regularity as effectively 'proved' for practical purposes, and avoid language that suggests metaphysical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Laplace-style formulas to quantify probability of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that an event will repeat is conditioned by past repetitions. Laplace's results are cited: an event occurring p times without failure has been asserted by Laplace to have probability p/(p+1) of occurring again; more generally if it has happened p times and failed q times, the probability of happening next time is (p+1)/(p+q+2) (odds (p+1) to (q+1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing new phenomena, apply appropriate probabilistic reasoning grounded in prior frequencies (individual and class experience). Use numerical examples (solidification of hydrogen vs. sun rising) to calibrate belief: rare single experiments yield far weaker probabilities than phenomena observed extremely often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle reported miracles/anomalies by weighing past frequencies (practical negligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If breaches in routine (miracles/anomalies) are exceedingly rare (e.g., one authenticated breach per 1000 million routines), the odds against such a miracle occurring next are about 1000 million to one; such odds make belief in the miraculous irrelevant to practical conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat well-authenticated breaches as possible but, unless supported by sufficient frequency, practically negligible when guiding action. Adopt high evidentiary standards for claims of routine breaches and factor in base rates when evaluating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theories as conceptual tests of perceptions; revise when perceptions diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories (e.g., gravitation) yield conclusions of logical necessity within conception and can be used to test perceptions; if sense-impressions differ from these conclusions, the theory isn't valid as a descriptive account of the routine of perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories by comparing their predicted routines with observed perceptual routines. If disagreement appears, treat it as evidence the theory's descriptive scope is insufficient and revise or replace the theory rather than transferring conceptual necessity to perceptions.
